podcasts.name: Latent Space
podcasts.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
podcasts.description: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Enjoy! We covered: * Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. * Ian’s rule that biology

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: The Changing Physics of Cybersecurity and Drug Development with OpenAI President Greg Brockman
podcasts.description: Technology has always been the fundamental driver of improvement for human quality of life. And with the recent rollout of advanced frontier models, like OpenAI’s GPT-6, humanity can now massively accelerate scientific discovery for its benefit. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil are joined by OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman to discuss the company’s rapid progress across frontier models, cybersecurity, and scientific discovery. Greg shares how nearly 400 century-old math problems have been solved using its AI agents, and how the technology has the potential to transform other fields like biology in the realm of drug discovery. He also talks about how proactive, always-on AI agents like Dots impact modern productivity, why he believes the best UI is no UI at all, how cybersecurity is in a critical window of time to use peak intelligence to find and fix vulnerabilities in systems, and why OpenAI remains committed to keeping humans in the driver’s seat even as models surpass us in capability. podcasts.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
podcasts.title: Jev: The AI That Makes Decisions, Not Text - and Why It Changes Everything (Diogo Almeida)
podcasts.description: What is Jev? TypeSafe’s Jev is a new kind of AI model, a “decision model,” that doesn’t write text. It makes fast, cheap, calibrated decisions inside software, and it has taken the AI world by storm: within weeks of launch it became the most copied model in AI, with OpenAI, Cloudflare, Amazon and Databricks all shipping their own versions, and TypeSafe just raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. In this episode, Jev’s creator Diogo Almeida, co-inventor of RLHF at OpenAI and now CEO of TypeSafe, explains Jev in plain English: what a “System One” or decision model actually is, why ChatGPT-style language models can’t be trusted inside software (“95% Einstein, 5% Mr. Bean”), how RLHF and RLVR created the problem, what RLCD (reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions) does differently, where the training data comes from, which models Jev is built on, why “just a classifier” is a compliment, and why he calls pre-training “a giant dumpster fire of wasting resources.” We also cover the copycats and why he thinks they missed the hard part, why benchmarks are useless, whether Jev will go open source, the Jevons paradox business model behind the name, why he doesn’t believe AI is on the path to recursive self-improvement, and why he thinks the AI winter he feared has been averted. (00:00) Cold open & Intro: “95% Einstein, 5% Mr. Bean” (01:09) Jev’s breakout launch: why intelligence per dollar matters (03:25) Why TypeSafe built in stealth for two years (05:50) “We could have had AGI last year” (06:48) Why the product carries the marketing (09:33) What is Jev? Machine-native AI, built for software (10:53) System One vs. System Two: the limits of reasoning (12:26) From simple decisions to composable AI (15:21) Automating email: giant prompts vs. smart if-statements (20:03) Probabilities, thresholds, and developer control (23:43) Why Jev is faster and cheaper than chat models (25:39) “Classification is AI-complete” (27:16) RLHF: how OpenAI trained models to please humans (31:28) Sycophancy, refusals, and the hidden costs of RLHF (34:22) RLVR: why benchmark gains don’t mean reliable automation (37:51) RLCD: optimizing for machine-native intelligence (39:54) Why TypeSafe builds its training data in-house (41:49) The Bitterest Lesson: define the task before scaling (44:39) Building Jev from open-weight models (45:56) Is Jev just a classifier? Why that’s a compliment (48:35) “Build prod, not God” (50:11) Embedding AI in software, beyond coding assistants (53:05) Jev’s copycats: matching the interface vs. the intelligence (55:33) Why benchmarks mislead the users they should help (58:37) Open weights vs. APIs: how TypeSafe weighs the tradeoff (1:00:04) Jevons paradox: a new market for machine intelligence (1:02:50) Why Diogo is skeptical of recursive self-improvement (1:04:47) Can practical automation avert an AI winter?

podcasts.name: AI & I by Every
podcasts.title: How Hugging Face’s Investor Spots Winners
podcasts.description: Check out Gemini Audio: https://goo.gle/Every-Gemini-Audio Bet on founders who understand the technology, because their first idea probably won’t be the one that sticks. That’s the view of Matt Hartman, founder and managing partner of Factorial Capital. In 2016, as a partner at Betaworks, Hartman was part of the team that wrote the first check into Hugging Face, which was then a chatbot app for teenagers. Today it’s the largest hub for open-source AI, and Nvidia has agreed to buy it for about $13 billion. On this week’s episode of The Every Podcast, Hartman tells Natalia Quintero how backing Hugging Face shaped his investment thesis, how Factorial grew into a “family tree” of technical founders who help him scout deals, and why vibe-coding his own app gave him a new respect for SaaS. podcasts.title: Education is Failing our Students in this AI-Driven World
podcasts.description: Schools and universities are failing to adapt to our modern world, in which AI is becoming increasingly pervasive in all aspects of life and work. In fact, AI may be changing what should be considered foundational knowledge that all students must learn. In this Fully Connected episode, Daniel and Chris explore the role of AI in education and the future of learning. They note the bureaucratic inhibitors to educational reform, and the fact that classroom teachers don’t have the authority to innovate and personalize the learning process for their students, and discuss how AI tools can support personalized learning while preserving critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills.
